391.event_title: Gandhi reads Unto This Last and founds the Phoenix Settlement
391.place: Johannesburg to Durban, and Phoenix, Natal, South Africa
391.event: In 1904 Mohandas Gandhi's friend Henry Polak gave him John Ruskin's Unto This Last to read on the overnight train from Johannesburg to Durban. Gandhi later wrote that he could not put the book down, could not sleep that night, and resolved to change his life according to its ideals. Within weeks he moved the press of his newspaper Indian Opinion to a farm near Durban, the Phoenix Settlement, where he and co-workers such as Albert West lived and worked together as equals.
391.explanation: Gandhi did not treat the book as information to be admired; he reorganised his work and daily life around it almost at once, and later translated it into Gujarati as Sarvodaya.
391.tie_back: The kural asks that one learn what is worth learning thoroughly and then stand in conduct that fits it, which is exactly what Gandhi did after one night's reading.
391._accuracy_note: A very close fit for the second half of the kural, living by what one has learned; the first half, learning without flaw, is shown less directly.

392.event_title: Al-Khwarizmi writes on the Hindu art of reckoning
392.event: Working at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad under the caliph al-Ma'mun, the mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a treatise explaining the Hindu place-value numerals, including zero as a placeholder, and how to calculate with them. The Arabic original is lost, but a Latin translation, Algoritmi de numero Indorum, carried these numerals and methods into Europe. The Latin form of his name, Algoritmi, is the origin of the word algorithm.
392.explanation: A single book on how to write and work with numbers gave much of the world the counting system it still uses for trade, science and computing.
392.tie_back: The kural calls number one of the two eyes of human life, and al-Khwarizmi's treatise opened that eye for whole civilisations.
392._accuracy_note: A strong example of number as a way of seeing the world, but it shows only one of the kural's two eyes, number, and not letters.

393.event_title: Louis Braille devises a reading system for the blind
393.place: Royal Institute for Blind Youth, Paris, France
393.event: Louis Braille, blinded as a small child, entered the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris in 1819, where the library held only a few cumbersome books in embossed letters. Adapting a raised-dot system shown to the school by Charles Barbier, he worked out by the age of 15 a code of six-dot cells that blind people could read quickly with their fingertips and write with a simple tool. He published the system in 1829, and it was later adopted around the world.
393.explanation: Braille's code gave blind people direct access to reading and writing, showing that the power to learn does not depend on physical sight.
393.tie_back: The kural says that only the learned truly have eyes, and Braille, who could not see, gave countless blind people those eyes of learning.
393._accuracy_note: Matches the traditional commentary that a learned person without sight still has eyes, though the kural's harsh image of the unlearned is not illustrated.

394.place: Kobe, Tokyo, Kyoto and other cities, Japan
394.event: At the invitation of the publisher Kaizosha, Albert Einstein toured Japan from 17 November 1922, having learned during the voyage that he had been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. Crowds and journalists met him at Kobe, and audiences packed auditoriums in several cities to hear him lecture on relativity for three or four hours at a time through an interpreter. At Keio University in Tokyo on 19 November about 2,000 people filled the lecture hall.
394.explanation: The tour shows how a great scholar's presence and talk could draw and delight ordinary people far beyond the circle of specialists.
394.tie_back: The kural says the mark of the learned is that people rejoice to meet them and think of them after they part, and Japan's welcome to Einstein shows that gladness.
394._accuracy_note: Captures the joy of meeting a learned person, but the crowds were drawn partly by fame, and the longing after parting is not documented in the sources used.

395.event_title: Frederick Douglass trades bread for reading lessons
395.event: As an enslaved boy in Baltimore, Frederick Douglass was taught the alphabet by Sophia Auld until her husband forbade the lessons. In his 1845 Narrative, Douglass recorded that he then made friends with the white boys he met in the street and turned as many as he could into teachers, giving bread to the hungry ones in return for lessons. He also taught himself to write by copying letters from ship timbers and a schoolboy's copy-books.
395.explanation: Douglass sought learning from anyone who could give it, however young or humble, and his literacy became the foundation of his later life as a writer and abolitionist leader.
395.tie_back: The kural praises those who eagerly seek learning, like the needy before the rich, and Douglass begged lessons from street children with whatever he had to offer.
395._accuracy_note: A vivid picture of eager, unashamed learning; the kural's image is of humility before an established teacher, which differs somewhat from Douglass's improvised lessons.

396.event: Michael Ventris became fascinated by the undeciphered Linear B script at the age of 14, after visiting a 1936 London exhibition of finds from Crete and meeting Sir Arthur Evans there. Though he trained as an architect, he kept studying the tablets for years and from 1949 worked intensively on them, using careful analysis of how signs recurred and combined. In June 1952 he announced on British radio that the script recorded a very early form of Greek, a result confirmed with the linguist John Chadwick.
396.explanation: Years of patient study let Ventris see what experts had missed, pushing written Greek back centuries before Homer.
396.tie_back: The kural compares understanding to water in a sand well that rises as one digs deeper, and Ventris's insight came only after about sixteen years of steady digging into the problem.
396._accuracy_note: Illustrates understanding growing in proportion to sustained study, though the kural speaks of learning in general rather than a single problem.

397.event_title: Al-Idrisi makes his home at the court of Roger II of Sicily
397.event: Muhammad al-Idrisi, a Muslim scholar born in Ceuta in North Africa and educated in Cordoba, entered the service of the Norman Christian king Roger II of Sicily around 1145. He lived and worked at the court in Palermo for the rest of his life, gathering reports from travellers and earlier geographers. Shortly before Roger's death in 1154 he completed a world map with an accompanying geography, known in Arabic as the Book of Roger.
397.explanation: Al-Idrisi's learning made him welcome and honoured in a foreign kingdom of a different faith, where he produced one of the great geographical works of the Middle Ages.
397.tie_back: The kural says every land becomes the learned person's own land, and al-Idrisi found a lasting home at a foreign court because of what he knew.
397._accuracy_note: A close fit for the kural's first half, learning as portable citizenship, while its second half about learning until death is shown only implicitly.

398.event_title: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine teaches doctors for six centuries
398.place: Persia (now Iran), and universities across Europe
398.event: The Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, compiled al-Qanun fi al-tibb, the Canon of Medicine, in the early 11th century. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, it became a standard medical textbook in European universities and was still used at Montpellier, France, as late as about 1650. It also remained central to medicine in the Islamic world.
398.explanation: The learning gathered in one lifetime went on guiding and protecting physicians and patients for many generations after its author's death.
398.tie_back: The kural says the learning of one life protects through seven more, and Ibn Sina's Canon kept serving long after him, much as Kalaignar reads it of later generations.
398._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the kural speaks of learning protecting its owner across future births, while this shows learning benefiting later generations, which matches only the secular reading.

399.event: Rabindranath Tagore, who had won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, started an experimental school at Santiniketan in 1901. In 1921 he expanded it into Visva-Bharati, a world university whose stated aim was a meeting of the cultures of East and West. The institution became a central university of India in 1951, and Santiniketan was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
399.explanation: Tagore turned his own delight in literature, music and art into an institution meant to share that delight with students from across the world.
399.tie_back: The kural says the learned love learning all the more when they see it delight the world, and Tagore built a university to spread to the world the learning that delighted him.
399._accuracy_note: Shows learning shared for the world's joy, but the kural's inner cycle of deepening love for learning is Tagore's own experience, which the sources do not document directly.

400.event_title: China's universities carry their learning to Kunming in wartime
400.event: After the outbreak of war with Japan in 1937, Peking University, Tsinghua University and Nankai University left their campuses in the north, regrouped first in Changsha and then moved to Kunming in the far southwest. There they operated together as the National Southwest Associated University in poor, makeshift buildings until 1946. Among its students were Chen-Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957.
400.explanation: The universities lost their buildings, libraries and homes, yet the knowledge of their teachers and students survived and produced some of the century's great scientists.
400.tie_back: The kural calls learning the one wealth that cannot be destroyed, and the wartime university showed that when everything else was left behind, learning travelled on intact.
400._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of learning outlasting material loss, though the kural's contrast with all other wealth is shown only by implication.
